resources.string: Android asks you to allow a keyboard twice: once to add it, and again to choose it. Both steps are below.
1. Add Folio Keys in Android\'s settings

Android warns that a keyboard can see what you type. That is true of every keyboard — the system sends it your keystrokes. Folio Keys asks for no permissions at all, including no Internet permission, so what it sees cannot leave this phone.
Not added yet. Step 1 opens the list Android keeps of the keyboards it allows.
Added. Use step 2 to switch to it — some phones put their own keyboard back afterwards, so check it comes up in the field below.
Added, and in use. Tap the field below to see it.
Emoji you use will show up here

Folio Keys remembers words you type that it does not already know — names, places, the way you spell things — so it stops suggesting something else instead. It is kept on this phone, never from a password field, and never from an app that asks it not to.
Forget the %1$d words it has learned
It has not learned any words yet
A row above the keys offering words. Never in a password field.
Replaces a word that is not a word, when one word is clearly what you meant. Never changes a real word, and backspace puts back exactly what you typed. Off when suggestions are off.
Remembers words it does not know, so it stops suggesting something else instead. Never from a password field, or from an app that asks it not to.
Capital at the start of a sentence
Only where the app asks for it.
Two spaces after a word become a full stop and a space.
Digits on their own row instead of behind the 123 key. Costs a row of height.
é, ñ, ü and the rest. The digits in the corners of the top row still work either way.
Show the letter above your finger
A short tap when a key goes down.
Sound and vibration also follow the phone\'s own settings, so turning them on here cannot turn them on there.
Flick a key down for its corner character
The digit printed on the top row, without waiting for a long press. It is already on the keycap, so nothing is hidden.
Flick a letter up for a capital
Faster than shift for a single letter.
Every gesture needs a deliberate journey, so the drift of typing fast is never mistaken for one.
How much of the screen the keys take. Taller is easier to hit; shorter leaves more of what you are typing into.
Following the phone is what almost everyone wants.
Two halves under two thumbs. Automatic splits on a screen big enough in both directions — unfolded, or a tablet — and not on a phone lying on its side.
Swipe the space bar to move the cursor
Needs a deliberate journey, so a drifting thumb still types a space.
Swipe left on backspace for a whole word
Swipe down on the space bar to hide
The chevron in the corner does the same thing.
A short word that stands for a longer one: type it, and the phrase is offered first in the strip. It is only ever offered — nothing is replaced until you tap it.
What it stands for, e.g. on my way
A shortcut needs a single word and something different for it to stand for.
Pushes the keys and their labels as far apart as they go, rather than the softer greys of the ordinary palette.
